title: Object and possessive pronouns
objectives: Select object pronouns after verbs and prepositions.
Choose possessive pronouns when the noun is understood.
Distinguish possessive pronouns from possessive determiners.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A pronoun is a word that can replace a noun or noun phrase. Object pronouns are me, you, him, her, it, us and them. We use them after a verb when they refer to the person or thing receiving an action: ‘I know Sara’ can become ‘I know her’. We also use object pronouns after prepositions such as with, for and to: ‘Come with us’.

Possessive pronouns show who something belongs to. They are mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs. They can replace a possessive determiner and noun when the noun is clear: ‘This is my coat’ can become ‘This coat is mine’. The word its can be a possessive determiner before a noun; a standalone possessive pronoun its is very rare and is not practised here.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: The subject pronouns are I, you, he, she, it, we and they. The object forms are me, you, him, her, it, us and them. Compare ‘She knows me’ with ‘I know her’. The subject normally comes before the main verb in a statement; an object pronoun can come after the verb. You and it have the same form in both lists.

Possessive determiners come before nouns: my bag, your bag, his bag, her bag, our bag, their bag. Possessive pronouns normally stand without the noun: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. His has the same form in both patterns: ‘his bag’ and ‘The bag is his’. Do not add an apostrophe to hers, ours, yours or theirs.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Look at the examples below. ‘Can you help me?’ asks for help for the speaker. ‘I can help you’ offers help to the person addressed. In ‘The teacher is speaking to them’, them follows the preposition to. The correct form depends on the pronoun’s role in the sentence.

In a conversation, a noun can be omitted when both people know what it is: ‘Is this your jacket?’ ‘No, it’s hers.’ Here hers means her jacket. The possessive pronoun avoids repeating jacket. A pronoun needs a clear reference, so include the noun or a name if the listener might not understand who or what you mean.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use a subject form after an ordinary verb in the patterns taught here: say ‘I can see him’, not ‘I can see he’. After a preposition, say ‘for them’, not ‘for they’. The pronoun refers to the same people, but its grammatical form changes.

Do not put a noun after mine, yours, hers, ours or theirs in this pattern: say ‘my coat’ or ‘the coat is mine’, not ‘mine coat’. A sentence such as ‘This is her’ identifies a person, while ‘This is hers’ identifies something that belongs to her. Context helps you choose the intended meaning.

examples.sentence: I know Anna. I see her every day.
examples.note: Her replaces Anna as the object of see.
Me is the object of calls.
Them refers to the people receiving help.
Mine means my bag; the noun is understood.
Yours asks whether the seat belongs to the listener.

common_errors.reason: Use the object pronoun her after see.
Use my before the noun coat.
The possessive pronoun theirs has no apostrophe.

summary: Use object pronouns such as me, him and them after verbs and prepositions.
Use possessive determiners before nouns and possessive pronouns without a following noun.
Use context to make the person or thing a pronoun refers to clear.
